premise: A disease catalogue is a screen: entities carry aggregate scores estimated from a varying number of observations. This library's argument therefore applies to its own reference data, and these are the results of applying it.

findings.name: Ascertainment bias
findings.mechanism: A gene is found in diseases that are studied, and diseases are studied when there are patients to study. So 'has a known gene' is partly a measure of attention, not of tractability.
findings.test: Rank correlation between phenotype annotations (a proxy for attention) and whether a causal gene is known.
findings.detail: Median annotations: 19 for diseases with a gene, 10 for those without (9,028 vs 3,648 diseases).

findings.name: The streetlight effect
findings.mechanism: Looking where the light is. The rarer a disease, the fewer patients exist to sequence, so the less likely its cause has been found — which means a catalogue read naively says rare diseases are less genetic. They are not; they are less studied.
findings.test: Rank correlation between prevalence band (rarest first) and whether a causal gene is known, across Orphanet diseases with a stated prevalence.

findings.name: Panel coverage masquerading as biology
findings.mechanism: A cell type that was measured for more genes has more chances to be some gene's maximum. So a chart of 'disease genes peaking in this cell type' may be a chart of how deeply each cell type was sequenced.
findings.test: Rank correlation between the number of genes measured in a cell type and the number of disease genes peaking there.
findings.detail: Across 154 cell types. This tests a chart THIS PROJECT already drew (the cell-burden bar chart in the world atlas).

findings.name: Varying observation count
findings.mechanism: Genes per disease ranges over orders of magnitude. Any ranking of diseases by an aggregate over their genes is therefore partly a ranking of how many genes each has — which is this repository's founding claim, applied to its own reference data.
findings.detail: min 1, median 1, p95 3, max 114 across 11,030 diseases — a spread of 114x.

findings.name: Missing not at random
findings.mechanism: Prevalence is absent for a reason correlated with everything else: a disease nobody has counted is usually one nobody has studied. Treating 'Unknown' as a neutral category averages two different populations together.
findings.test: Share with a known gene, among diseases with a stated prevalence versus those without.
findings.detail: 56% of the 5,324 with a stated prevalence have a gene, against 42% of the 1,404 without.

findings.name: Survivorship of the catalogue itself
findings.mechanism: Every disease here is one somebody described, named and got accepted into a reference. Diseases too rare to have been seen twice, or seen only where no catalogue reaches, are absent — and absent in a way no statistic computed FROM the catalogue can detect.
findings.test: Not testable from this data. Stated so it is not mistaken for absent.
findings.detail: The denominator of every percentage on this page is the catalogue, not the world. Nothing here can measure that gap.
